notes: Part 1 extradition adjournment and appeal; Field J dismissed appeal but extended required period under section 36.

enrichment.short_title: Handa: Part 1 extradition adjournment, appeal and required-period extension
key_facts: Mr Handa, a French national serving a 30-month UK sentence for burglary and assault, faced a Part 1 warrant from Paris for murder and theft allegedly committed in December 2003.
Both the issuing authority and Mr Handa sought adjournment of the extradition hearing until his domestic release date of 4 May 2005.
District Judge Wickham refused adjournment under section 23 and ordered extradition on 15 October 2004, citing the gravity of the French allegations.
Mr Handa challenged the refusal to adjourn by judicial review and appealed the extradition order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined judicial review and appeal to the High Court against refusal to adjourn a Part 1 extradition hearing and against the extradition order.
enrichment.outcome: Substantive appeal dismissed; no order on judicial review; court agreed under section 36(3)(b) that the required period should run from 4 May 2005 with liberty to apply.
enrichment.ratio: Ordering extradition before the end of domestic custody does not require discharge where surrender will not occur until release; where both parties sought adjournment and UK law lacks any provision to interrupt a domestic sentence for extradition, refusal to adjourn may be Wednesbury unreasonable, but an agreed extension of the required period can cure the practical injustice.
legal_issues: Whether section 34 bars judicial review of Part 1 extradition decisions
Whether refusal to adjourn under section 23 was irrational
Whether extradition could properly be ordered before domestic custody ended
Whether the court could extend the required period under section 36(3)(b)

notes: Landmark conflict-of-laws appeal on whether NSW MACA damage caps are substantive or procedural.

enrichment.short_title: Harding v Wealands: foreign tort damages caps as substantive law

statutes_considered.title: Motor Accidents Compensation Act 1999 (New South Wales)

key_facts: Mr Harding was rendered tetraplegic in a motor accident in New South Wales caused by Ms Wealands, an Australian national later served in England.
After liability was admitted, the parties tried a preliminary issue on whether NSW law, including MACA caps and restrictions, governed quantum.
Elias J held English law applied under section 12 or, alternatively, that MACA provisions were procedural and not applicable in England.
The defendant appealed, relying on MACA limits on non-economic loss, earnings, gratuitous care, interest and insurer credits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue trial on the applicable law governing assessment of damages in a foreign tort claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declarations made that NSW law governs all substantive issues and that MACA paragraphs 5(b)–(h) of the defence are substantive provisions to be applied to quantum.
enrichment.ratio: Statutory ceilings and restrictions on recoverable damages under the law of the place of the tort are substantive rather than procedural; an English court applies its own procedural rules but must give effect to foreign substantive limits on damages to avoid forum shopping.
legal_issues: Whether section 12 made English law substantially more appropriate for damages
Whether MACA quantification provisions were substantive or procedural
How Boys v Chaplin and Roerig v Valiant Trawlers apply after the 1995 Act
Whether foreign statutory damage caps bind an English court assessing quantum
linked_authorities: Roerig v Valiant Trawlers Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 21
John Pfeiffer Pty Ltd v Rogerson [2000] 203 CLR 503
Boys v Chaplin [1970] AC 268

confidence.notes: Final declarations and reasoning on the substantive/procedural distinction are explicit.

notes: Costs Judge summarily assessed arbitration costs to satisfy expiring bank guarantee wording.

enrichment.short_title: Rotary Watches: summary assessment of arbitration costs for security call
key_facts: Rotary Watches Ltd won a long ICC arbitration against impecunious US distributor Rotary Watches (USA) Inc and obtained 75% of its costs.
The arbitrator referred recoverable costs to the High Court under section 63(4) rather than awarding costs on account.
Security of £609,750 included Standard Chartered guarantees expiring on 31 December 2004 requiring a High Court costs certificate to trigger payment.
RWL offered to accept £609,750 in full settlement of its much larger claimed costs to avoid further dispute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application in the Costs Office for summary assessment, interim certificate or payment on account following an arbitration costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Summary assessment allowed at £609,750 with direction that a certificate issue forthwith to satisfy the Standard Chartered guarantee; payment-on-account and interim certificate applications refused.
enrichment.ratio: Once an arbitrator refers costs to the court under section 63(4), the court has discretion to summarily assess costs and, where justice requires, direct issue of a certificate even outside the usual detailed assessment framework; paying parties must still be allowed to raise points of dispute before an interim certificate.
legal_issues: Whether a Costs Judge may summarily assess referred arbitration costs
Whether CPR 44.3(8) or 47.15 permits interim relief before detailed assessment
Whether a summary assessment certificate can satisfy guarantee wording requiring assessed costs
Whether the claimed £609,750 was realistic on the arbitration papers

notes: Gypsy green-belt injunction appeal; suspension pending planning application overturned.

enrichment.short_title: Mid-Bedfordshire v Brown: gypsy site injunction and contempt of court
key_facts: Romany gypsies moved caravans onto agricultural green-belt land at Tingrith in flagrant breach of an ex parte injunction obtained on Bank Holiday Sunday 29 August 2004.
They submitted a retrospective planning application for a gypsy residential site after unlawful occupation began.
Tugendhat J granted a final prohibitory injunction but suspended it until planning determination, citing children's welfare.
The council appealed, arguing suspension rewarded contempt and undermined planning control.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against suspension of a section 187B planning injunction restraining unlawful residential use of agricultural land.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; suspension discharged; injunction suspended for four weeks only to allow the defendants to move off the land.
enrichment.ratio: Where occupiers deliberately breach a court order to create a fait accompli and then seek suspension pending a retrospective planning application, public interest in upholding court authority and planning control outweighs temporary humanitarian relief; only a short suspension to enable relocation is appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether suspension of a section 187B injunction pending planning determination was a proper exercise of discretion
Relevance of Article 8 and children's interests
Effect of flagrant breach of an existing injunction
Application of South Bucks DC v Porter and related gypsy-site authorities
linked_authorities: South Bucks District Council v Porter [2003] 2 AC 558
Davis & Ors v Tonbridge & Malling BC [2004] EWCA Civ 194
Coates & Ors v South Bucks DC [2004] EWCA Civ 1378

notes: Registered land forfeiture appeal; equitable assignee may forfeit before registration under section 141(2).

enrichment.short_title: Scribes West v Relsa: forfeiture by equitable assignee before registration
key_facts: Scribes West Ltd held a business lease of Kensington premises; Relsa Anstalt was registered freeholder until it executed a TR1 transfer of the reversion to Relsa Barkers on 28 February 2001.
Notice of assignment was given to the undertenant, but registration did not occur until 3 January 2002.
Relsa Barkers peaceably re-entered for rent arrears on 16 July 2001 and granted a new lease to Settle Up Ltd.
The lessee argued forfeiture was invalid because the transferee was not yet the registered proprietor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on whether a valid lease forfeiture could be effected after execution but before registration of a transfer of the reversion.
enrichment.ratio: Section 141(2) extends rent and covenant enforcement to the person entitled to the income of the land; an equitable assignee of the reversion who has given notice to the tenant is such a person and may forfeit even before registration of the legal title.
legal_issues: Whether section 141(2) covers only legal reversioners or also equitable assignees
Effect of non-registration under the Land Registration Act 1925
Application of Turner v Walsh and Schalit v Nadler
Whether an equitable assignment of rent suffices for forfeiture
linked_authorities: Turner v Walsh [1909] 2 KB 484
Schalit v Joseph Nadler Ltd [1933] 2 KB 79
Commissioners of Inland Revenue v John Lewis Properties Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 35

notes: Second appeal restored negligence claim against local authority after hostel fall; Gorringe/Sandhar principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Bluett v Suffolk: local authority duty after placing teenager at Foyer hostel
key_facts: Jennifer Bluett, aged 16½, jumped from a third-floor Foyer hostel window on 3 January 1998 to escape intruders who had broken down her door.
She suffered permanent incapacitating injuries; assailants were later convicted of GBH or affray.
Social worker Peter Lorford-Page helped place her at The Foyer in Ipswich after earlier unsuitable accommodation.
Summary judgment/strike-out applications had removed all defendants except Suffolk County Council before this second appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from strike-out/summary judgment dismissing negligence claim against Suffolk County Council.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim against the County Council to proceed subject to permission to amend on the framework set out in the judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Section 24 advise-and-befriend duties do not create a statutory cause of action, but a local authority social worker may owe a common law duty where a vulnerable child relies on him for accommodation advice and he assumes responsibility; on summary disposal the court could not conclude there was no real prospect that The Foyer's security risks were or ought to have been known.
legal_issues: Whether section 24 Children Act 1989 creates a private law duty of care
Whether Mr Page assumed responsibility for safe accommodation at The Foyer
Whether breach and causation were too speculative for strike out
Application of Gorringe, Sandhar and Caparo/Henderson principles to social services
linked_authorities: Gorringe v Calderdale Metropolitan Borough Council [2004] UKHL 15
Sandhar v Department of Transport, Environment and the Regions [2004] EWCA Civ 1140
X (Minors) v Bedfordshire County Council [1995] 2 AC 633

notes: CRHP reference; Collins J substituted erasure for unduly lenient 12-month GMC suspension.

enrichment.short_title: CRHP reference: erasure for GP convicted of manslaughter and domestic violence
key_facts: Dr Feda Mulhem, a Syrian-trained GP, pleaded guilty to manslaughter after fatally administering vincristine intrathecally instead of intravenously to a leukaemia patient in January 2001.
He also pleaded guilty to assaults on his wife and children, including a fractured elbow, and lied to hospital staff about injury causes.
Poole J sentenced him to 18 months' imprisonment and treated erasure as inevitable; the GMC Professional Conduct Committee imposed 12 months' suspension in his absence.
Dr Mulhem absconded, likely to Syria, and did not appear before the GMC.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court reference by the Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals alleging an unduly lenient GMC sanction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; suspension set aside and erasure from the medical register substituted.
enrichment.ratio: A conviction for manslaughter arising from gross negligence in clinical practice, combined with serious pre-existing domestic violence and dishonesty, is fundamentally incompatible with remaining a doctor; suspension was perverse where the doctor did not appear and gave no assurance of future safety.
legal_issues: Whether 12 months' suspension was unduly lenient for manslaughter and violent offences
Weight to be given to hospital system failures and sentencing judge mitigation
Application of GMC indicative sanctions guidance on erasure versus suspension
Appropriate sanction where the doctor did not participate in proceedings

confidence.notes: Unduly lenient finding and substituted erasure are clearly and fully reasoned.

notes: Appeal against 30-month sentence for attempting to influence juror; reduced to 21 months.

enrichment.short_title: R v Hardy: sentence for attempting to influence a juror

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: During a GBH trial at Nottingham Crown Court, Hardy approached a juror outside court and said 'Find them not guilty'.
The juror reported the encounter and the trial had to be aborted, wasting public money.
Hardy pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice on the basis the meeting was accidental rather than planned.
Judge Cole sentenced him to two and a half years' imprisonment despite remorse, early plea and old convictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence for perverting the course of justice by attempting to influence a juror.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentence reduced from 30 months to 21 months' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Interference with jurors warrants substantial custody, but sentence must remain proportionate to the nature and degree of interference; an unplanned encounter without threats or bribery, coupled with an early guilty plea, may justify a lower term than cases involving intimidation or conspiracy.
legal_issues: Whether 30 months was manifestly excessive for this offence on the pleaded basis
Distinction from section 51 intimidation of jurors
Relevance of aborted trial and wasted public expense
Appropriate sentencing level by reference to comparable authorities
linked_authorities: R v Williams [1997] 2 Cr App R(S) 221
R v Goult (1994) 4 Cr App R(S) 355
R v Watmore [1998] 2 Cr App R(S) 46

notes: Court of Protection receiver costs appeal; inter-office memos and bill-payment letter units reduced.

enrichment.short_title: Re Radcliffe: solicitor receiver costs and inter-office communications
key_facts: Mr Gordon Watson, a panel solicitor receiver, sought assessment of general management costs for a brain-injured patient over one year.
His bill included inter-office letters and memos between him and employee Ms Butterworth, and numerous short letters paying routine invoices.
Costs Officer Sainthouse disallowed internal communications and halved time allowed for payment letters, following earlier Garylee Grimsley and Jamie Walker decisions.
The receiver appealed, arguing the expanded PGO panel-receiver role justified wider remuneration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against detailed assessment of a Court of Protection solicitor receiver's general management bill.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed in substance; minor adjustments to document time and payment-letter allowances; final certificate slightly lower than the costs officer's figure.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor receiver cannot treat himself as instructing his own firm; inter-office liaison and routine supervisory discussions are firm overhead, while short bill-payment letters may be recoverable where Rule 87 is disapplied by standard Court of Protection practice for professional receivers, but only at a reduced unit rate unless the letter involves exceptional expenditure review.
legal_issues: Whether panel receivers may recover internal fee-earner communications
Whether routine bill-payment letters merit six-minute or three-minute units
Application of Rule 87 Court of Protection Rules 2001
Whether the 1995 Practice Note disapplies Rule 87 for solicitor receivers
linked_authorities: R v Legal Aid Board ex parte Bruce [1991] 1 WLR 1231
In the Matter of Tina Jayne Cloughton (Arden J, 1999)
R v Sandhu (Mustill J, 1984)

notes: Section 13 application; new inquest ordered after post-inquest expert evidence on treatment and cause of death.

enrichment.short_title: Bloom v Coroner: fresh inquest after hospital death from renal sepsis
key_facts: Carmel Bloom died aged 54 after treatment for a kidney stone at Bupa Roding Hospital and transfer to Whipps Cross intensive care following suspected septicaemia.
The coroner held an inquest in August 2003 and returned a verdict of death by natural causes, finding treatment appropriate.
Post-inquest expert reports from Dr Bristow and Mr Smith challenged adequacy of resuscitation, ambulance transfer and whether death was inevitable from septicaemia.
Bernard Bloom obtained the Attorney General's fiat for a section 13 application to quash the inquest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 13 Coroners Act 1988, with Attorney General's authority, to quash an inquest and order a fresh hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; original inquest quashed; new inquest ordered before a different coroner.
enrichment.ratio: Section 13 permits a fresh inquest where new expert evidence makes it necessary or desirable in the interests of justice, even if the coroner conducted the original hearing properly; if post-inquest material shows death may not have been inevitable and raises neglect or causation issues under the Article 2-compliant 'how and in what circumstances' inquiry, the family are entitled to a further investigation.
legal_issues: Whether the original inquest adequately investigated post-operative care and transfer
Whether the coroner should have called independent expert evidence
Whether new expert reports justify a fresh inquest under section 13
Application of Middleton and Jamieson to neglect verdicts and Rule 42
linked_authorities: R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] UKHL 10
R v HM Coroner for North Humberside ex parte Jamieson [1995] QB 1
In re Rapier (deceased) [1988] QB 26

confidence.notes: Court distinguished coroner criticism from section 13 threshold; fresh inquest rationale is clear.
